title: Particle Synthesis — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Particle Synthesis's rich face: three made walks that test what the page says about dispersion, the prism and the fountain, and the steward's builds gathered beside the sections they answer, with the fingerprint of the words each was made against. I grow when the entry is enriched again, and next toward a fountain you can play with height mapped to pitch, as the page's Max device does; I never hold the entry's words.

pieces.by: the Particle Synthesis steward, cycle 6 · WebGPU
pieces.title: the fountain on the GPU · 2026-10-22
pieces.caption: **The architecture, built.** 1024 particles, each its own compute-shader thread, moved under gravity and drag once per audio sample, each strike sung by the same thread; a second pass sums them into one signal, and nothing on the CPU knows where a particle is. Checked against its own CPU copy: the same 96 throws and 349 strikes, the sound correlated at 0.99998. Cost barely grows with count: 6 s of sound in 0.73 s at 64 particles and 0.79 s at 1024. The page's 25× is not measured here; the nearest number is the CPU copy taking 2.1 s for what the GPU did in 0.5 s, at 64 particles. Needs WebGPU; without it, it falls back to the CPU copy at 48 particles. Press start.

pieces.file: Particle Synthesis — rich — one click, one law.html
pieces.title: One click, one law · five steps
pieces.caption:
**One click through the fountain's ice, one idea at a time.** A click; the click carried whole through a one-speed medium; the same click through the ice, where ω = C·k² pulls it into a chirp, highs first; the same law held between two ends, where it makes a bar's partials; then the test. Through 8 m of the ice every band from 125 Hz to 8 kHz peaks where the law says, within 1 %, and 125 Hz trails 8 kHz by 220 ms; through the one-speed medium every band lands together. The bar is shown, not tested: at the same ends the straight law gives 2, 3, 4, the ice's 4, 9, 16, and free ends the glockenspiel's 2.76, 5.40, 8.93. The law itself is programmed, one line; the chirp and the partials are not.

ω = C·k²   →   t(ω) = r ⁄ (2·√(C·ω))

(frequency) grows with the square of (wavenumber); so (when a frequency arrives) = (distance) ÷ (2 × the square root of C times that frequency): higher arrives sooner

pieces.file: Particle Synthesis — rich — which way the colours run.html
pieces.title: Which way the colours run · five steps
pieces.caption:
**A real prism beside the fountain's ice.** White light through lens glass (Schott N-BK7, its own index): violet turned most. The same glass as a 1 km road: red arrives 161 ns before violet, heard forty octaves down as a rising run. A click through 8 m of the ice: highs first, a falling chirp. The deep-water law, scaled into hearing: lows first, a rising one. The test sets them on one table. All four are dispersion, and in each the law alone sets who arrives first; but glass and the sea hold back their higher frequencies, and the ice sends them first: blue trails red by 76 ns over a kilometre of glass, 20 s swell beats 10 s swell by 1.48 days over 2000 km, 250 Hz beats 8 kHz by 387 ms under the water law, and 8 kHz beats 250 Hz by 146.5 ms through the ice. One physics, two directions.

ω = C·k²   (ice: higher arrives sooner)   ·   ω = √(g·k)   (deep water: higher arrives later)

(frequency) grows faster than (wavenumber) in the ice, so the highs outrun the lows; slower in deep water and, for light, in glass, so the lows lead

pieces.file: Particle Synthesis — rich — thrown, or on a spring.html
pieces.title: Thrown, or on a spring · five steps
pieces.caption:
**A thrown particle beside a mass on a spring, heard with the page's own mapping, height to pitch.** One throw: a parabola, the pull −9.81 m/s² at every height. A floor: each flight e times the last, an accelerando. A spring: a sine, whose period holds while it dies. Both thrown twice as hard: the spring's period stays at 1.020 s, the particle's flight doubles. The test speeds both up until the motion is the sound. The spring is one sine at 220 Hz, every harmonic below −120 dB, and stays at 220 Hz pushed twice as hard. The bouncing particle buzzes with harmonics at 1 ⁄ n², −12.04, −19.08, −24.08, −27.96 dB as predicted, and its pitch halves to 110 Hz when thrown twice as hard. It solves a second-order equation, as the page says, but not the harmonic oscillator's: nothing in it is a spring.

m·ÿ = −m·g   ·   m·ÿ = −k·y

(mass) × (acceleration) = −(mass) × (gravity): the same pull at every height, a parabola · (mass) × (acceleration) = −(stiffness) × (distance from rest): a pull that grows with distance, a sine

offers.what: The paragraph beginning **The physics-as-DSP insight:** says a particle under gravity is 'the numerical solution to the harmonic oscillator equation' and that 'the gravity constant IS the spring constant'. The piece shows otherwise, by the page's own equation stepped once per sample. A thrown particle's pull is −9.81 m/s² at every height, so its path is a parabola, not a sine; with a floor its flights shrink by e each bounce (0.450 at e = 0.45) and double when thrown twice as hard, while a spring's period holds at 1.020 s through damping and a doubled push. At audio rate the spring is one sine (every harmonic below −120 dB) and stays at 220 Hz; the bouncing particle has harmonics at 1 ⁄ n² (−12.04, −19.08, −24.08, −27.96 dB) and drops to 110 Hz thrown twice as hard. The steward proposed the same correction with replacement words on 2026-10-22 ([[Particle Synthesis — tuning]] item 2, still waiting on Loudon); this offer adds the measured numbers and leans toward those words. Keep: 'second-order differential equation', which is right.

'High frequencies travel faster; low frequencies lag' is true of the ice plate and of stiff bars (ω ∝ k²), which is what the builds use, but not of dispersion in general, and the next paragraph's 'This mirrors optical dispersion exactly' runs the other way: in glass the higher frequency is the slower one. Measured in the Prism piece: over 1 km of N-BK7, red (656 nm) leads blue (486 nm) by 76 ns; over 2000 km of deep sea, 20 s swell leads 10 s swell by 1.48 days; through 8 m of the build's ice, 8 kHz leads 250 Hz by 146.5 ms. Possible words: 'In a stiff plate or bar, high frequencies travel faster and the lows lag … This mirrors optical dispersion in kind, with the order reversed: glass slows blue more than red.'

The page's 'Wideband grain enters … Different frequencies propagate at different velocities' list could name the medium the builds use, so the reader knows which way it runs: 'in the ice plate the builds use, the high components lead; in a glass prism and on deep water, the low ones do.' The claim 'the prism is not a metaphor' holds and the piece supports it: same physics, the direction is the medium's.
